slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 13, use 13.1.2 Understanding References as Aliases as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. An alias is another way to access the same object. Observing a mutation through the original name and through the reference should therefore give the same stored value. This differs from a copy, which is an independent object with its own state. Avoid turning that mental model into unsupported layout claims. A reference may be implemented with a pointer-like mechanism in some contexts, or optimized away in others; its specified semantics are what matter. You cannot treat a reference as a separately reseatable pointer object. Use a pointer or reference wrapper when a design genuinely needs an indirect access path that can change targets. slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 13, use 13.2.1 Modifying Caller-Owned Data as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. A nonconst reference parameter makes mutation possible and should be used when changing the caller’s object is part of the operation’s purpose. Name that purpose clearly, such as apply_offset(readings, amount). Validate prerequisites before making partial changes whenever a failure would leave the caller in an inconsistent state. Two reference parameters can alias the same object unless the interface forbids it. A function that assumes distinct objects may fail when called with the same argument twice. State and test aliasing assumptions. For simple arithmetic updates, a local temporary can sometimes make the behavior correct even when input and output refer to the same object. slides.title: 13.2.2 Avoiding Expensive Copies
keyPoints: Passing a large container as a const reference avoids copying its elements merely to inspect them.
The function borrows the container for the call and must not retain that reference beyond the owner’s lifetime.
A const reference also avoids mutation through that particular parameter.
The benefit depends on type and use.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 13, use 13.2.2 Avoiding Expensive Copies as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. Passing a large container as a const reference avoids copying its elements merely to inspect them. The function borrows the container for the call and must not retain that reference beyond the owner’s lifetime. A const reference also avoids mutation through that particular parameter. The benefit depends on type and use. Passing a small integer by const reference often adds indirection without useful savings. If a function needs to take ownership of a value or store an independent copy, a value parameter may express that requirement more naturally. Modern move semantics later make ownership transfer efficient; references should not be used to disguise an operation that actually needs ownership. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.title: 13.3.1 Using const References
keyPoints: A const reference prevents modification through that access path.
It does not make the object globally immutable if another nonconst alias exists.
It also does not automatically make concurrent access safe: another thread changing the object without.
Const references can bind to some temporaries, with lifetime-extension rules that depend on the exact context.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 13, use 13.3.1 Using const References as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. A const reference prevents modification through that access path. It does not make the object globally immutable if another nonconst alias exists. It also does not automatically make concurrent access safe: another thread changing the object without synchronization can still cause a data race. Const references can bind to some temporaries, with lifetime-extension rules that depend on the exact context. Do not generalize those rules into “a reference keeps anything alive.” A function storing a reference to a temporary argument can leave a dangling member after the full expression ends. Prefer owning storage when an object must retain data after a call. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.title: Failure clinic — A failed operation left half the data changed
keyPoints: A stronger offset function rejects values that would exceed a permitted range.
If it updates early elements before checking later ones, failure can leave a mixed state.
A caller that retries with another offset may then apply the operation to an already partly changed collection.
The all-or-nothing repair validates every candidate first.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 13, use Failure clinic — A failed operation left half the data changed as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. A stronger offset function rejects values that would exceed a permitted range. If it updates early elements before checking later ones, failure can leave a mixed state. A caller that retries with another offset may then apply the operation to an already partly changed collection. The all-or-nothing repair validates every candidate first. Only after that phase succeeds does mutation begin. For fixed integer bounds, safe precondition comparisons can avoid forming an overflowing addition. The lab’s solution pattern checks positive offsets against the upper bound and negative offsets against the lower bound before performing any addition. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 13, use Borrowing boundary as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. Do not keep first across an operation that might reallocate the vector. A reference cannot be checked against null to determine whether its target is still valid. Its validity must follow from the owner and operation sequence. slides.narration: This is a chapter listing, not a detached toy. Before running or reading it, state what behavior the program is supposed to witness. Two Names Referring to the Same Object gives us an executable slice of Chapter 13. The expected stdout is not decorative; it is the behavioral witness for this example. The first visible line is '25 25'. If there are multiple lines, read them in order because order often encodes loop progression, branch selection, or state changes. Expected stderr is empty, which means normal behavior is being reported through stdout rather than the diagnostic channel. Expected exit code is 0, so the operating system sees the run as successful after the program finishes printing. If the displayed output ever differs after an edit, do not jump straight to 'wrong.' Ask which requirement changed, which path executed, and whether the difference belongs on stdout, stderr, or the process status.
